papers.title: Mind-wandering preserves word-level coupling while disrupting comprehension
papers.abstract: Readers can move their eyes through a page but retain little of its meaning when their minds wander. We tested whether word properties still guide their eyes during these lapses. We analyzed public eye-tracking and electroencephalography (EEG) data from 44 adults who read articles. They marked the text read during each lapse they noticed. We linked these spans to the sentences needed for later comprehension questions. Word frequency, length and surprisal still predicted which words readers skipped and how long they looked at them. Compared with on-task reading, these effects met equivalence bounds of $\pm$10% for skipping and $\pm$20% for gaze duration. Readers spent 14.6% longer on words during lapses. Yet readers answered less accurately when lapses covered sentences needed for a later question. The adjusted difference was 25.7 percentage points for lapses covering all versus none of these sentences. The fixation-related EEG response was 42.7% smaller during lapses. At left posterior-lateral sensor P7, the median increase in alpha power was 10.0%. Occipital sensor Oz showed no reliable increase. These results suggest that word properties can guide the eyes while readers fail to form or retain a useful representation of the text.

papers.title: Same currents, different field: $\Delta f = 0$ carrier-only stimulation is not temporal interference without the beat
papers.abstract: Carrier-only stimulation ($\Delta f = 0$) is generally considered the most rigorous control for temporal interference (TI) stimulation, assumed to reproduce TI's kilohertz carrier field without its low-frequency beat. We show that this assumption is incorrect: without the frequency difference, the carrier fields interfere coherently, changing the peak strength, power, and direction of the resulting field depending on electrode polarity and montage geometry. Using computational field modeling, we demonstrate that these mismatches can be substantial and widespread. We therefore recommend that TI studies report electrode polarity, model both carrier-field exposures, and choose controls according to their study objectives.

papers.title: Prototypes of the Mind: A Unified Framework for Probing the Visual Brain
papers.abstract: Deep learning has driven substantial progress in modeling fMRI responses, yet most existing approaches are optimized for a single objective---such as neural encoding, stimulus decoding, or post hoc interpretation---making it difficult to obtain a coherent account of neural representations. We introduce a unified framework that connects vision foundation models to brain activity while supporting neural analysis from multiple complementary perspectives. Our approach replaces black-box features with a sparse, interpretable representation composed of visual prototypes, and links these prototypes to voxel responses through a linear readout. This design makes the model transparent at both levels: prototype activations expose the visual concepts present in the stimulus, while the learned linear weights characterize each voxel's selectivity. Using this interface, we identify which visual concepts drive neural responses and where they appear in the image, reveal cortical organization through voxel tuning in prototype space, and perform controlled stimulus synthesis to probe cortical selectivity through targeted interventions. Together, these results establish prototype-based representations as a unified and interpretable foundation for studying visual representations in the human brain.

papers.title: Analysis choices decide whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1: a multiverse analysis of model-brain RSA
papers.abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival trained networks as models of visual cortex, and we had reported an untrained-network advantage over backpropagation at V1 in THINGS fMRI, together with a dependence on evaluation resolution. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the untrained network scored below the trained one at every pooling grid (median r difference -0.043 at g = 4, 0 of 5 seeds positive), and also in MSE skill and per-fold r. In exploratory analyses, across 36 combinations of unit normalisation, distance measure and voxel normalisation (28 distinct analyses), the sign of the V1 contrast depended on the analysis (intervals above 0 in 5 and below 0 in 9 distinct analyses), and in our networks the resolution dependence of the original convention appeared in only one cell. Raw correlation-distance representational similarity analysis (RSA) covaried with the alignment of model and voxel patterns with the unit-mean profile (Spearman 0.97 across our networks, 0.79 across six ImageNet architectures); the advantage was absent from the component orthogonal to the mean profile, and the parallel component alone did not resolve it. On the unweighted angular component of centred patterns, trained networks were ahead at V1 (our network and 5 of 6 ImageNet models) and at LOC (all seven); the norm-weighted angular term was not resolved. A luminance-and-contrast bank scored above every network under ridge (point estimates), and adding network features under a shared penalty did not improve prediction. Intervals are stimulus-bootstrap intervals for three subjects, and 6 pre-stated predictions were not met. We recommend reporting sensitivity to centring over the evaluated stimuli on both sides, reporting components separately, and including a small multiverse and simple baselines.

papers.title: Optogenetic Modulation Fraction: A Robust Opsin-Presence Effect and an Unresolved Cell-Type Question, by Censoring-Aware Survival Analysis of Public Neuropixels Data
papers.abstract: Expressing channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in an interneuron population substantially raises the fraction of locally recorded units whose spike timing is altered by light, relative to no-opsin controls, under every method tried. Establishing that result rigorously, and retracting two secondary claims that did not survive the same rigor, is this paper's actual content. We reanalyze eight public Allen Institute Neuropixels sessions (4,112 units), modeling light-to-first-spike latency as a right-censored time-to-event outcome, with a Cox model, pooled FDR correction, and a small-cluster-robust test (logistic regression plus an exact wild cluster bootstrap, since only eight session clusters exist). We report an unrestricted modulation fraction and a restricted direct-responder fraction (evoked latency under 10 ms, an explicit, literature-grounded threshold). ChR2-expressing Sst/Pvalb sessions show a large, bootstrap-confirmed elevation over control under both metrics. Two further claims, each initially suggested by a standard test, did not survive the exact bootstrap or a direct formal check, and we report both retractions as results in their own right. Vip-ChR2's apparent elevation over control is not confirmed by the bootstrap and becomes non-significant once restricted to direct responders. A second pattern, that among modulated units Vip sessions had a higher proportion of direct responses than Sst/Pvalb, opposite the raw ordering, evaporated under the same bootstrap test: no genotype contrast approaches significance, and control has the highest proportion of all three, which cannot be biological. Per-session rates vary enormously within one genotype. With two earlier corrections (a session-composition artifact and a standard-versus-exact-bootstrap discrepancy), this is a four-correction paper: pooled estimates and secondary patterns deserve the same scrutiny as a headline claim.

papers.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
papers.abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

papers.title: Dynamical mean-field theory of latching Potts networks
papers.abstract: Spontaneous transitions between memories, as observed in internally generated cognition such as mind-wandering and free association, require neural dynamics capable of destabilizing one attractive memory state and moving towards another. We ask what minimal representational structure is required for such transitions to emerge in random associative networks. To address this question, we study Potts associative networks with $S$ active states per unit and slow adaptive thresholds. The $S=1$ case can model a standard Hopfield-like network of binary units. We employ dynamical mean-field theory in the extensive-load regime, where the number of stored patterns scales linearly with network size and connectivity, and we focus on transitions between two condensed memories, which are singled out in the connectivity matrix. In the finite-load regime, we show that transitions are governed by an effective drive term, whose sign and temporal evolution distinguish high-latching (structured), low-latching (random), and non-latching regimes. The resulting phase diagram shows that adaptation alone is not sufficient: transitions only occur within certain ranges of the overlap between the two memories. In the binary case $S=1$, in particular, no unit can be active in both memories but in different Potts states, thus strongly supressing the high-latching, structured transitions that exist for $S>1$. In the extensive-load regime, non-condensed memories generate colored fluctuations and retarded self-interactions through an effective memory kernel. We find that latching trajectories change the effective timescale of this kernel, a dynamical signature of transitions in the extensive-load regime. These results indicate that multi-state Potts-like representations are essential for structured memory-to-memory transitions, a hallmark of spontaneous thought.

papers.title: Random Exploration is Random
papers.abstract: Decision making often requires balancing exploitation of familiar options with exploration of uncertain alternatives. One strategy for exploration is random exploration, in which choices become more variable and less tied to the option that currently appears best. However, it remains unclear whether this variability reflects genuine stochasticity or instead a deterministic structure that traditional cognitive models fail to capture. We examined this question using the Horizon Task in an aggregated dataset of 1,392 participants completing over 1,270,695 trials. In this task, exploration becomes more valuable when participants have more future choices, and choice variability increases under longer horizons. We tested whether more expressive neural network models could recover deterministic structure from this additional variability. Although neural networks provided better overall fits to behavior than the traditional model, long-horizon choices remained consistently less predictable than short-horizon choices. These findings show that limited model expressiveness cannot fully account for the increased variability associated with random exploration, suggesting random exploration truly is substantially random.

papers.title: Parameter Symmetries Determine Representational Geometry in Overparameterized Nonlinear Networks
papers.abstract: Representations are routinely used across machine learning, psychology, and neuroscience to draw inferences about the computations of biological and artificial systems. Such inferences presume that the geometry of these representations reflects the computation being performed. For artificial neural networks, however, the extent to which the function a network computes constrains this geometry remains unclear. One key obstacle is that these networks admit parameter symmetries: changes in parameterization that preserve function exactly while reshaping representational geometry. Here, we show that a broad class of parameter symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication, and scaling. This feature-level characterization yields a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components, revealing how representational degeneracy can exist without and grows with overparameterization even when function is held fixed. Finally, we establish conditions under which implementation-level selection rules resolve this degeneracy, yielding identifiable geometries in which features are weighted according to their contributions to the network's function. Together, our results delineate when representational geometry can support inferences about computation, and when it cannot.

papers.title: Alignment De-Identifies Without Aligning: A Congruence-Invariant Relational Gap in Cross-Subject Neural Representations
papers.abstract: In brain-computer interfaces, inter-subject variability remains a major challenge that limits decoding performance across users. Subject-wise alignment is widely used to improve cross-subject transfer of neural decoders, yet it is typically evaluated only through decoding accuracy, which cannot determine whether aligned representations share greater task-related structure. We therefore distinguish two questions that accuracy conflates: whether alignment removes subject-specific information and whether it makes the relational organization of task conditions more similar across individuals. Using three motor imagery-EEG cohorts, trials are represented as covariance matrices and aligned by recentering each subject's mean covariance to a common reference. Subject-specific information is quantified with a subject-identification probe, whereas relational structure is assessed using representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) computed from condition means with the affine-invariant Riemannian distance. We show that recentering leaves this distance, and therefore the resulting RDMs, unchanged. Consistent with this result, recentering reduces subject identification accuracy from 0.96 to chance level across all cohorts, while altering RDMs only at numerical precision. Cross-subject agreement in relational structure is significantly above zero but below the estimator's lower noise ceiling. Introducing an explicit similarity regularizer during training also fails to increase held-out agreement: the apparent reduction in between-subject differences is explained by a decline in the reliability ceiling rather than improved alignment. These findings show that eliminating subject identity is not equivalent to aligning relational geometry. More broadly, alignment claims must be interpreted relative to the invariances of both the distance and the statistic used to evaluate them.

papers.title: Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks
papers.abstract: Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(\omega)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(\tau)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(\omega)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.

papers.title: Similarity-Guided Optimization Strategies for Approximate Network Symmetry Detection
papers.abstract: Symmetry in complex networks is a structural property with broad implications for network function, dynamics, and robustness. While classical approaches rely on exact automorphisms and thus remain highly sensitive to small perturbations, recent work of Liu has introduced approximate formulations that relax the strict invariance condition and recast symmetry detection as an optimization problem over permutations. We investigate how node-level similarity information can be used to bias the search toward structurally plausible vertex correspondences, with network centralities serving as one interpretable instance. Building on this perspective, we adapt simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, tabu search, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution and the quadratic symmetry approximator to this problem, add similarity guidance to each, and introduce Bilinear Approximate Symmetry Inference (BASIN), which learns a soft assignment matrix via bilinear embeddings. Using a unified evaluation pipeline, we compare their guided and unguided variants, BASIN and a random baseline on four synthetic graph families, structural brain connectomes, and three empirical networks with known automorphism groups. Node-similarity guidance is decisive where a planted orbit exists that the unguided search misses, and algorithm-dependent elsewhere, on synthetic and empirical networks alike. Overall, tabu search achieves the strongest performance; its guided variant (SGTS) has the lowest median score among the guided variants in all 44 synthetic conditions, while BASIN is the better of the continuous relaxations on rewired lateral graphs. The effect of node-similarity guidance is therefore regime-dependent rather than uniformly positive.

papers.title: On the minimum energy required to trigger a spike
papers.abstract: We formulate and numerically study the problem of finding the minimum energy required to trigger a spike in a three-dimensional conductance-based excitable model. The variational formulation seeks a state trajectory that reaches the boundary of the spiking region with the least \textit{peak} cumulative work supplied through the membrane port. We approximate voltage histories by sums of real exponentials, reducing the problem to a finite-dimensional optimization. The best-found voltage waveform consists of a hyperpolarization phase followed by a depolarization phase, which seems to match the experimentally determined optimal stimulus in squid giant axons.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Dynamics on Arbitrary Time Scales
papers.abstract: The leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron combines a passive membrane law with threshold-triggered firing and reset. We formulate this hybrid neuron model, under constant input, on an arbitrary Hilger time scale $\mathbb{T}$. Our central result is that, after the first spike, the firing times satisfy $t_{n+1}=\Pi_{\mathbb{T}}^{+}(t_n+T_c)$, where $T_c$ is the classical reset-to-threshold travel time. This recursion requires no periodicity, homogeneity, or translation invariance of $\mathbb{T}$; it holds for every time scale that is unbounded above. To preserve the passive membrane physics, we use the inverse cylinder transformation to construct a positively regressive coefficient $p_m$. The resulting delta-dynamic equation is exactly the restriction to $\mathbb{T}$ of the classical continuous-time LIF trajectory. By contrast, the direct transcription $V^\Delta=-(V-V_\infty)/\tau_m$ exhibits graininess-dependent sign reversal and amplification at coarse right-scattered points. The first firing time is the forward projection of the classical continuous threshold-crossing time onto $\mathbb{T}$, and, when the graininess is bounded by $\mu^\ast$, the per-event forward-projection delay -- from each reset to the next realized firing time, relative to the continuous crossing time computed from that same reset -- is bounded above by $\mu^\ast$. On $\mathbb{T}=h\mathbb{Z}$ we obtain the explicit lattice-quantized law $T_{\mathrm{ISI}}^{(h)}=h\lceil T_c/h\rceil$, which converges to the classical continuous-time inter-spike interval as $h\to0^+$. The framework therefore separates preserved membrane physics from the temporal opportunity structure imposed by the time domain. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic Hilger-calculus treatment of a threshold-and-reset LIF spiking neuron on an arbitrary time scale.
